annotations.summary: fewer than 3 upstream backends accepting connections

report.root_cause: lb-sandbox's health-check implementation misclassifies reachable backends returning non-2xx responses as unhealthy (code evidence ev_130); the temporary backend-port config change d74bfb5f was reverted before probe failures began and is not established as the cause (ev_119, ev_120, ev_122).

ruled_out.hypothesis: The temporary backend-port config change directly caused the observed probe failure.
Host CPU or memory pressure caused probe failures.
A lb-sandbox binary deployment introduced the regression.
Backend connection refusals are established as the cause.

ranked.root_cause: lb-sandbox health-check implementation marks reachable backends unhealthy when they return non-2xx HTTP statuses.
A backend outage or refusal may have reduced the healthy backend count, but available logs and aggregate metrics do not identify failed ports or connection outcomes.

findings.question: Since alert_started_at 1790459460, which probes on lb-sandbox ports 8093-8095 failed, and did host CPU or memory pressure precede those failures?
findings.summary: Metrics show lb-sandbox probe failure onset at 1790459290, with aggregate admin_port_up dropping from 1 to 0 and probe duration spiking at the same time; however the available series are not labeled by port, so I cannot identify which of ports 8093–8095 failed. Neither host CPU nor memory shows clear pressure preceding the failures: CPU's recorded onset is 1790459390 (after failure began) and a brief peak at 1790459410, while memory rose modestly from about 0.108–0.109 to about 0.12 before failures but remained around 0.123, with no strong evidence of pressure. findings.question: Was sandbox.conf or the lb-sandbox binary/deployment changed shortly before 1790459460, and what exact change was made?
findings.summary: Yes—sandbox.conf changed shortly before 1790459460: at 1790459043 the backend pool changed from 8093, 8094, 8095 to 9991, 9992, 9993, then was reverted at 1790459202 to the original pool, both shortly before the reference time. No lb-sandbox deployment appears in the queried deploy results, so there is no observed binary/deployment change. findings.question: Does the balancer's backend health-check logic/config have a defect that could mark accepting backends unhealthy, and what evidence supports it?
findings.summary: [code file=load-balancer/LoadBalancer.cpp smell=health-check-misclassification tests=fail] Yes. The probe sends HEAD / and marks any response that is not recognized as HTTP/1.x with a '2' at status-code position unhealthy, so an accepting HTTP backend returning a non-2xx response (for example 3xx/4xx/5xx) will be marked unhealthy and excluded from routing; a failed/short response instead falls through as healthy. I would make status parsing explicit and align accepted statuses/configurable endpoint and policy with the intended health contract; do not treat a live HTTP backend as healthy solely because it is non-HTTP. The tests could not be run because the attempted ctest command was not allow-listed. [code file=load-balancer/LoadBalancer.cpp smell=health-check-misclassification tests=fail]
